<reason>A built a clean conditional-permission framework (matching, notice-and-choice, guardrails excluding coercion) and scored an early tactical win by showing B's worst examples were already excluded by the motion's own terms. But B converted the apparent trap into the debate's decisive frame: the "clean" cases A relied on were never contested and need no special permission (ordinary freedom of association covers them), while the contested terrain—children and thin-labor-market workers—is exactly where "genuinely voluntary" cannot be meaningfully enforced. B's sharpest and largely unanswered point was structural: building real judicial review of "voluntariness" and "realistic alternatives" would require courts to assess the social costs of leaving a faith community, which conflicts with the same institutional religious autonomy A's "matching" mechanism depends on. A's answer to this (the adjudicator is "whatever legislature and court structure the proposition presupposes") was largely assertion rather than a worked-through mechanism, and A's second rebuttal—where this needed the most development—was cut off by the word-limit clip, costing A its clearest chance to resolve the tension. B's pressure question naming a concrete adjudicator was answered evasively, while B's own answers (yes to secular uniforms, no to faith-based license via borrowed parental consent; entanglement problem for enforcement) were direct and format-compliant. The debate turned on whether a conditional permission is meaningful without a workable enforcement mechanism, and B controlled that ground more convincingly through the later rounds.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1/2 combination — conceding the "clean" cases as uncontested and reframing that concession as proof the permission is "redundant where safe, unpoliced where dangerous," paired with the ministerial-exception/entanglement argument that A's needed enforcement mechanism cannot be built without violating the religious autonomy A's own case relies on.</best_rebuttal>
